label: GIMUN rules · Hero
title: Rules of procedure.
lead: GIMUN follows standard Model UN parliamentary rules, built to keep debate moving and open to first-time and experienced delegates alike.

label: GIMUN rules · The debate (always shown)
title: How a debate runs.
lead: Five stages, the same in every committee, from roll call to the final vote.

items.title: Roll call and quorum
items.body: The chairs read the country roster. Answer 'Present' to keep the right to abstain on resolutions, or 'Present and voting' to give it up and vote Yes or No. Quorum is one third of assigned countries. Tip: say 'Present' if you may need to stay neutral.

items.title: General speakers list
items.body: Speeches of 90 seconds by default; the list stays open across sessions. Finish early and you must yield your remaining time. Tip: yielding to points of information shows command of your position.

items.title: Caucuses
items.body: Between speeches, move a moderated caucus to debate one sub-issue, or an unmoderated caucus to negotiate, draft clauses and merge blocs. Tip: keep a moderated caucus topic narrow so speeches stay concrete.

items.title: Drafting a resolution
items.body: Blocs combine preambulatory and operative clauses. Once the chairs approve format and mandate, the text gets a draft resolution code and is introduced to the room. Tip: two or three active authors amend faster than a long sponsor list.

items.title: Voting
items.body: A two-thirds motion closes debate and the doors close. Amendments are voted first, then draft resolutions in the order they were tabled. Tip: in a roll-call vote you may pass once; on the second call you must vote.

label: GIMUN rules · Motions (always shown)
title: Motions and points, in order.
lead: When several motions are raised at once, the chairs take them in this order of precedence.

label: GIMUN rules · Yields
title: Three ways to yield.
lead: Finish a speech before your time runs out and you must give the floor back in one of these ways.

items.title: to the chair
items.body: Your remaining seconds return to the chairs. The floor reopens for motions or the next speaker, and no questions may be put to you.
items.meta: The delegate of France yields the remaining time to the chair.

items.title: to another delegate
items.body: Your time passes to an ally, who may accept or decline. If they accept, they speak for the remainder but cannot yield again.
items.meta: I yield my remaining time to the distinguished delegate of Japan.

items.title: to points of information
items.body: The floor may question you. The chairs recognize non-argumentative questions, and answers come out of your remaining time.
items.meta: I yield my remaining time to points of information.

label: Moot rules · The memorials (always shown)
title: Submitting memorials.
lead: Soft copies go through the memorial submission link; the hard copies come with you.

items.title: Both sides
items.body: One memorial on behalf of the petitioner(s)/appellant(s) and one on behalf of the respondent(s).

items.title: Soft copy
items.body: A .pdf of each memorial, sent once the memorial submission link is provided after your team registers. A memorial in any other format, or split across files, loses 1 mark.

items.title: Hard copies
items.body: Three hard copies of each memorial, printed on one side only, handed in on arrival. Each missing copy costs 1 mark; no hard copies means disqualification.

items.title: Covers and identity
items.body: Petitioner memorials have a blue cover and respondent memorials a red one. Only the team code may identify the team, and the hard copy must match the soft copy exactly, or the team is disqualified.

items.title: Preliminary rounds
items.body: 5 December. Teams are matched by draw of lots on 4 December, after the inaugural ceremony. Each team argues twice, once as petitioner and once as respondent, and never meets the same team twice. Held if enough teams register.

items.title: Quarter-finals
items.body: 5 December. Qualification goes by rounds won, then winning difference, then memorial marks. 20 minutes per team; pairings by draw of lots.

items.title: Semi-finals
items.body: 6 December. Quarter-final winners, paired by draw of lots. 35 minutes per team.

items.title: Final
items.body: 6 December. The two semi-final winners, 45 minutes per team. The winner of the final wins the competition.

items.title: Ties and scouting
items.body: A tie in the quarter-finals, semi-finals or final is decided on preliminary round marks, and memorial marks never decide a round. Teams may not watch another team’s oral rounds unless they have been knocked out; scouting means instant disqualification.

label: Moot rules · The format
title: What a memorial must look like.
lead: Citations follow {citation}. Speaking footnotes and endnotes are not allowed. Only the team code may identify the team.

items.title: Pages
items.body: Cover page, table of contents, list of abbreviations, index of authorities, statement of jurisdiction, statement of facts, issues raised, summary of arguments, pleadings/arguments advanced, prayer.

items.title: Cover
items.body: The case line, side of the memorial, year of competition and name of the court, with the team code in the top right corner.

items.title: Type
items.body: Single-spaced footnotes, 1-inch margins on all sides, hard copies printed on one side only.

label: Moot rules · In the courtroom
title: Fifteen minutes in the preliminaries.
lead: Each team's time includes rebuttal and sur-rebuttal, if the judges permit. Arguments must keep to the issues in the memorial, and the judges' decision on each round is final.

items.title: per team
items.body: In the preliminaries, split between the speakers as the team decides, with at least 7 minutes each.

items.title: rebuttal
items.body: A rebuttal may take no more than 2 minutes.

items.title: points
items.body: The maximum per speaker per judge. The researcher may sit with the speakers, and a compendium may be handed up only if the bench permits.

label: Moot rules · The scoring (written memorial criteria; points in Meta)
title: How memorials are scored, out of 100.
lead: Memorial marks do not decide the result of any round. They break a tie when teams qualify from the preliminaries to the quarter-finals.
